summary: Interpret multiplication as scaling (resizing): for a positive quantity, the size of the product relative to that quantity depends on whether the OTHER factor (a positive multiplier) is greater than, equal to, or less than 1. Multiplying 7 by 5/3 enlarges it, by 1 (e.g. 4/4) leaves it unchanged, by 2/5 or 3/4 shrinks it. This confronts the 'multiplication always makes bigger' belief and lets learners judge a product's size WITHOUT computing (3/4 × 7 is part of 7, so less than 7). It also unifies with equivalence: multiplying by n/n = 1 (n not zero) rescales the name without changing the value. Emphasise predicting direction before calculating and comparing the multiplier to 1 — not whether it is written as a fraction.
misconceptions: 'Multiplication always makes the number bigger' (and division always smaller) — predicts 3/4 × 7 > 7 (Fischbein's primitive intuitive model; named explicitly in the IES guide).
Over-corrects to 'any fraction makes it smaller' — predicts 5/3 × 7 < 7 because the multiplier is written as a fraction, ignoring that 5/3 > 1.
Thinks multiplying by n/n changes the value (because 'you multiplied'), not recognising n/n = 1.

activities.title: Stretch-and-shrink bar: predict before you scale
steps: Look at a 7-unit bar placed beside a faint marker of the original length 7.
Before anything moves, predict out loud or in writing whether scaling by a chosen multiplier will make the bar longer, shorter, or the same, and say WHY.
Set the multiplier to 3/4 and watch the bar contract to sit short of 7 (3/4 × 7 = 5.25).
Set the multiplier to 5/3 and watch the bar stretch past 7 (5/3 × 7 ≈ 11.67).
Set the multiplier to 4/4 and watch the bar hold exactly at 7, re-partitioned to show it is still the same length.
Sweep the multiplier dial slowly across 1 and notice the exact point where the bar flips from shrinking to growing.
State the rule: multiplying a positive quantity makes it bigger only when the multiplier is more than 1.
activities.insight: For a positive quantity scaled by a positive multiplier, the product is larger than, equal to, or smaller than the quantity exactly according to whether the multiplier is greater than, equal to, or less than 1 — the number 1 is the pivot, not whether the multiplier is written as a fraction.

activities.title: Predict and sort multipliers by direction
steps: For each of 3/4 × 7, 5/3 × 7, 2/5 × 7, and 4/4 × 7, predict without calculating whether the product is greater than, less than, or equal to 7, and give a reason.
Sort a set of multipliers into three groups: 'makes bigger', 'leaves the same', 'makes smaller'.
For a prompt such as 'is 3/4 × 7 greater, less than, or equal to 7?', choose and justify an answer, and explain why 'greater, because multiplying makes bigger' is not correct.
Estimate the rough size of a product on a scale before revealing the exact value.
activities.insight: Deciding a product's direction is a comparison of the multiplier to 1, which can be done reliably before any arithmetic.

activities.title: Find the counterexample to 'multiplying always makes bigger'
steps: Consider the claim 'multiplying a number always makes it bigger.'
Find a specific case that shows the claim is false and explain why it fails (e.g. 3/4 × 7 is three-quarters OF 7, so less than 7).
Then state the corrected, precise rule: multiplying a positive quantity makes it bigger only when the multiplier is greater than 1; by 1 it stays the same; by less than 1 it gets smaller.
Explain why 5/3 × 7 does make 7 bigger, so the rule is about size relative to 1, not about being a fraction.
activities.insight: Refuting the over-generalised belief requires producing a counterexample and restating the condition precisely, which strengthens understanding of why the threshold is 1.

activities.title: Multiplying by n/n keeps the value
steps: Predict what 7 × 4/4 equals and whether it is bigger, smaller, or the same as 7.
Show on a bar or number line that 4/4 is one whole, so the length holds while being re-partitioned into quarters.
Connect this to fraction equivalence: multiplying a/b by n/n (n a whole number greater than 1) gives a different name for the same value.
Explain why 3/4 × 2/2 names the same value as 3/4.
activities.insight: Multiplying by n/n is multiplying by 1: it rescales the name (re-partitions) without changing the value, which is exactly what underlies equivalent fractions.

checkQuestion: Without working it out: is 3/4 × 7 greater than 7, less than 7, or equal to 7 — and WHY? Then tell me, again without calculating: does multiplying 7 by 5/3 make it bigger or smaller, and does multiplying 7 by 2/5 make it bigger or smaller?
checkAnswer: 3/4 × 7 is LESS than 7 (three-quarters OF 7 is part of it, and 3/4 < 1). 5/3 × 7 is BIGGER than 7 (5/3 > 1); 2/5 × 7 is SMALLER than 7 (2/5 < 1). The product's size depends on whether the multiplier is greater or less than 1.
